experimental-unit.def: The individual (person, animal, plant or object) to which a treatment is assigned in an experiment. Experimental units that are people are called subjects.

treatment.def: A specific condition imposed on experimental units. A factor is an explanatory variable in an experiment; its levels are the values it is set to.

control-group.def: A group that receives no treatment, a placebo or the standard treatment, to compare with the treatment group. A placebo is a fake treatment; the placebo effect is a response to it caused by expectation.

random-assignment.def: Using a chance process to decide which experimental units receive which treatment, so that other variables are balanced between groups on average.

replication.def: Using enough experimental units in each treatment group that chance differences between units tend to average out.

blinding.def: Keeping subjects (single-blind) or both subjects and the people who interact with them or measure the response (double-blind) from knowing who received which treatment.

completely-randomized.def: An experimental design in which every experimental unit is assigned to a treatment at random, with no grouping first.

block-design.def: A randomized block design groups experimental units that are similar in a way expected to affect the response into blocks, then assigns treatments at random within each block.

matched-pairs.def: A design in which units are put in pairs of similar units and chance decides which unit of each pair gets which treatment, or each unit receives both treatments in a random order.

statistically-significant-diff.def: A difference between treatment groups is statistically significant when it is too large to be explained by the chance variation of random assignment alone.
